nameStory: Orange hawkweed goes by many colorful nicknames that hint at its bold appearance and reputation. 'Devil's paintbrush' suggests someone dipped a brush in orange paint and dabbed it across the landscape, while 'fox-and-cubs' evokes a family of red-orange foxes nestled together in the meadow.
description: Orange hawkweed is a low-growing perennial wildflower that creates patches of brilliant orange-red blooms in fields and roadsides. The plant stays close to the ground with a rosette of fuzzy, spoon-shaped leaves, sending up stems 8-16 inches tall topped with clusters of vibrant daisy-like flowers. Originally from the mountains of Europe, this hardy plant has made itself at home throughout New England, often spreading to form colorful colonies.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant orange-red blooms about an inch across, shaped like small daisies with many narrow petals that feel papery to the touch. The flowers cluster together at the top of the stem, creating a fiery bouquet effect.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Fuzzy, blue-green leaves arranged in a flat rosette at ground level, shaped like elongated spoons. Run your fingers over them to feel the soft, almost velvety texture from tiny hairs covering both surfaces.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stays low to the ground in a spreading rosette pattern, with flower stems rising 8-16 inches above the leaves. Often forms patches or colonies connected by underground runners.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Flower stems are hairy and feel rough when rubbed, usually leafless or with just a few small leaves. The stems often have a reddish tinge and may branch near the top to hold multiple flower clusters.

habitat: Orange hawkweed thrives in sunny, open areas with poor to average soil, making it common along roadsides, in old fields, pastures, and disturbed ground. You'll often spot it in areas where the grass is thin or the soil has been compacted, as it tolerates harsh conditions better than many native plants. It particularly loves acidic soils and can be found from sea level to mountain elevations throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge early, forming fresh green rosettes as the weather warms. The fuzzy leaves are often the first sign of the plant awakening from winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from late May through August, with the most spectacular orange displays in June and July. Individual flowers last about a week, but new ones keep opening in succession.
seasonality.fall: Blooming winds down by September, though scattered flowers may appear into early fall. The basal leaves remain green and fuzzy, preparing to overwinter.
seasonality.winter: The rosette of leaves often stays partially green under snow, pressed flat against the ground. Look for the distinctive fuzzy, spoon-shaped leaves in protected spots during winter thaws.

funFact: Orange hawkweed can reproduce without pollination through a process called apomixis, essentially cloning itself through seeds that are genetic copies of the parent plant—meaning every orange hawkweed in a patch could be genetically identical!
confusionNotes: The brilliant orange color makes this plant hard to confuse with anything else in New England, though it might be mistaken for orange marigolds or calendulas in gardens. However, those garden flowers have much larger, fuller blooms and lack the distinctive fuzzy basal rosette of leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its beautiful flowers, orange hawkweed is considered an invasive species in North America, outcompeting native plants in fields and meadows. In its native European mountains, it's actually a protected species, showing how a plant can be treasured in one place and problematic in another.
compareHints: Orange hawkweed stands out from its hawkweed relatives by its distinctive orange-red flowers—most other hawkweeds in New England have yellow blooms. Mouse-eared hawkweed and yellow-devil hawkweed share the fuzzy leaves and low growth habit, but their bright yellow flowers make them easy to distinguish from the fiery orange devil's paintbrush.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mouse-eared hawkweed stands out from its hawkweed relatives by its distinctively fuzzy, silvery leaves and single yellow flowers on leafless stems.
Meadow hawkweed differs from its orange hawkweed cousin by having yellow flowers instead of orange-red ones.
Smooth hawkweed towers above its mouse-eared hawkweed cousin, which stays close to the ground in creeping mats with densely fuzzy leaves.
Yellow-devil differs from orange hawkweed by its yellow (not orange-red) flowers and generally paler, more silvery-fuzzy leaves.
Yellow Devil differs from Orange Hawkweed by its yellow (not orange-red) flowers and more tightly clustered flower heads.
